chapter_theme: Under the heading புகழ்தலின் கூறுபாடு, four verses on praise given out of place: praising oneself before the work is done, accepting praise even from one's own people, praising boasters who have nothing to boast of, and withholding the good word from a poor kinsman set apart among many kin.

65.reading: When the work they undertook has not come off even a little and they cannot yet know its outcome truly, people who praise themselves as having reached full success are like those who say they will sell at a fraction the birds still in the field.
65.nuance: The fault is timing as much as vanity: the praise runs ahead of a deed not yet accomplished, so it is a claim on a result that may never come, as birds in the field are not yet anyone's to sell. Line 2 (மெய்யா உணரவும் தாம்படார்) is hard to construe; it is read here as 'they have not come to know it truly', i.e. the outcome is still unknown.

pazhamozhi.literal: saying 'we will sell, at an eighth of the price, the birds that are still out in the field'

story.act: no story; the proverb is the boast of a seller who prices birds he has not caught

pazhamozhi.applied_to: self-praise before the work is done is a sale of what one does not yet have

66.reading: Even when it is one's own people who praise one, one should not settle into it but push it away, the verse tells the man of the bamboo hills, for those who wear ornaments do not put on jewels that do not fit them even if the jewels are their own.
66.nuance: The proverb turns on தமவேனும்: the jewels are one's own as the praisers are one's own kin (தமர்), and ownership does not make either fit. Praise is treated as something worn, to be refused when it does not sit on the wearer's measure. The address வெற்ப is the akam vocative for a hill chief, used here without any love situation.

pazhamozhi.literal: those who adorn themselves do not wear ornaments that will not fit them, even when the ornaments are their own

story.act: no story; the proverb is the ordinary practice of anyone dressing in jewels

pazhamozhi.applied_to: praise from one's own kin is to be refused when it does not fit

67.reading: To extol those who have no eminence from mother or father yet speak themselves up with the mouth, though it does no harm, is like calling the dog that curls up at the edge of the hearth a tiger.
67.nuance: The verse blames the praiser, not only the boaster: the one who echoes a hollow self-report names a hearth dog a tiger. It concedes that the flattery is harmless (நோயின்று), so the fault is falsity and absurdity, not injury. மிகவின்றி with தாயானும் தந்தையாலானும் is read as 'without distinction through either parent'; it could also mean 'not much esteemed even by their own mother and father', which makes the boasters people even their parents do not rate.

pazhamozhi.literal: saying of the dog that lies curled at the hearth's edge that it is a tiger

story.act: no story; the proverb names a timid house dog given a tiger's name

pazhamozhi.applied_to: praising self-proclaimed men of no standing gives a great name to a small thing

68.reading: A man among his many kin who does not attend to one of them, does not know him well, and keeps him apart because he is poor, like one who in speaking holds back the generous word from him, commits the painful wrong of drawing a line within a single row.
68.nuance: The proverb pictures a row (நிரை), most naturally a line of kin seated to eat or gathered together, within which one is marked off; the wrong is the partiality inside a body that should be one. The verse fits its heading on praise through line 3: the poor kinsman is denied the good word (வளவியசொல்) the others get. பார்த்துறான் in line 1 is obscure; it is read as 'does not look to him', and the syntax of lines 1-3 is loose.

pazhamozhi.literal: a distinction drawn within the row is painful

story.act: no story; the proverb names any line of people in which one is set apart

pazhamozhi.applied_to: singling out a poor kinsman for lesser regard among kin is a wrong

links.note: Naladiyar 340 says learning and birth win honour when others praise them but bring mockery when a man praises them himself; Pazhamozhi 65 condemns self-praise of a deed not yet accomplished.
links.teaches: Read together they give two grounds against self-praise: the quatrain's man owns real merits and is still mocked for voicing them, while Pazhamozhi's man claims a result that does not exist yet, so the second fault is falsehood on top of vanity.
links.list_adds: its proverb of selling uncaught birds adds the time element the quatrain lacks: praise claimed before the work is done is a sale of what one does not have.

links.note: Naladiyar 219 ranks abuse above praise of qualities one does not have; Pazhamozhi 66 says praise must be pushed away even when it comes from one's own kin.
links.teaches: The quatrain makes unfit praise worse than abuse in general; Pazhamozhi carries the refusal to the hardest case, the affectionate praise of one's own people, and gives the reason in the image of a jewel that is one's own and still does not fit.
links.list_adds: the proverb's own-but-unfitting jewel names the source the quatrain leaves open, one's own kin, and makes the test fit rather than giver.

links.note: 65 forbids praising oneself before the deed; 66 forbids settling into praise even from one's own people.
links.teaches: The two adjacent verses close off praise from both the self and the circle nearest the self, leaving only praise that fits the deed and comes from beyond one's own people as worth keeping.

links.note: Naladiyar 346 says the base man who gains a tiny fraction thinks himself Indra; Pazhamozhi 67 says those who extol such self-proclaimers call a hearth dog a tiger.
links.teaches: The quatrain describes the base man's inflated self-image; Pazhamozhi turns to the bystander who repeats it, so the pair shows the boast needs a flatterer to circulate and that the flatterer shares in the absurdity.
links.list_adds: it moves the fault from the boaster to the one who praises him and concedes that such praise is harmless, a qualification the quatrain does not make.

links.note: Kural 1047 says a man in poverty is looked at as a stranger even by his own mother; Pazhamozhi 68 calls it a painful wrong for a man to set a poor kinsman apart among his many kin.
links.teaches: The Kural records estrangement from kin as one of poverty's miseries; Pazhamozhi names the kinsman who does the estranging as at fault, so the same fact appears once as the poor man's suffering and once as the kin's wrong.
links.list_adds: its proverb of a line drawn within a row makes the poor kinsman's exclusion a breach of the group's own unity, which the couplet states only as the poor man's loss.

source_issues.issue: Line 2 (மெய்யா உணரவும் தாம்படார்) construes poorly; the reading is tentative.
பார்த்துறான் in line 1 is obscure and may be corrupt; lines 1-3 have loose syntax.
Parenthesised letters in அமரா(து) (66) and நோயின்(று) (67) are editorial restorations of elided sounds.
